Author: Gollan, Jennifer; Neilson, Susie
Title: Police chases are killing more and more Americans. With lax rules, it’s no accident
Abstract Note: Police chases kill nearly two people a day across the US, and the government is failing at nearly every level to address the growing problem.
Extra: The Chronicle spent months doing just that, building a database of fatal pursuits from 2017 through 2022 by filing more than 70 public records requests and examining information from research organizations, local news stories and court records. Reporters merged this data with records from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration to find that at least 3,336 people were killed as a result of police pursuits throughout the U.S. from 2017 through 2022. At least 15 of them were officers. More than 52,600 people were injured from 2017 through 2021, according to government estimates.

Author: Neilson, St John Barned-Smith, Susie
Title: S.F. mayor orders city to stop ticketing stolen vehicles after Chronicle story
Abstract Note: San Francisco Mayor London Breed orders city to stop ticketing stolen vehicles, instead recovering them, after Chronicle story
Extra: The Chronicle found that Municipal Transportation Agency (SFMTA) employees had ticketed approximately one-fifth of the 2,000 vehicles that were reported  Benjamin Fanjoy/Special to the Chronicle stolen to the city police force between May 1 and Sept. 17 and which remained listed as missing at the time parking officers encountered them. Breed ordered the SFMTA and the Police Department to work together to implement a system in which stolen cars are identified and recovered. San Franciscans will have to wait, however, before the directive becomes reality. City laws governing the use of surveillance technology — such as license plate readers — require multiple reviews by the city’s Committee on Information Technology, as well as a signoff by a supervisorial committee and a full vote of the Board of Supervisors. Board of Supervisors President Aaron Peskin said Wednesday that he asked City Attorney David Chiu to draft an ordinance amending the administrative code to allow the SFMTA to access data about stolen vehicles.
